To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the mental HRQOL is a strong predictor for estimated GFR (eGFR) decline in CKD patients.
the impaired mental HRQOL is associated with increased estimated glomerular glomerular filtration (eGFR) decline in CKD patients.
impaired mental health status in CKD patients is associated with eGFR decline.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of HRQL on CKD progression.
the impact of HRQL in CKD progression.
the relationship between impaired mental health and estimated glomerular filtrate rate decline, and the association between HRQOL and CKD progression in a cohort of CKD patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the impact of HRQL on CKD progression has not been well established.
there is a significant association between HRQOL and progression of CKD.
the association between mental health status and CKD progression remains inconclusive, and further prospective studies are required to confirm the findings.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the HRQOL in ESRD patients is significantly worse than in CKD patients and the HRQOL is significantly associated with mortality in both CKD and ESRD patients.
the HRQOL in the CKD population is associated with the rate of CKD progression.

impaired mental health status in CKD patients is associated with faster estimated glomerular filtrate (eGFR) decline, and deteriorated HRQOL is associated with increased all‐cause and cardiovascular mortality in CKD and ESRD patients.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HRQOL is associated with estimated GFR (eGFR) decline in a population with CKD.
HRQOL is associated with estimated GFR (eGFR) decline in patients with CKD, independent of traditional risk factors for CKD progression.
the HRQOL of patients with chronic kidney diseases is associated with estimated GFR decline.
